extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors learning mathematical proof writing; readers interested in mathematical exposition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and teaching mathematical proofs that are correct, clear, insightful, and pedagogically effective; intended to shape both practice and instruction. Emphasizes not just correctness but communication, understanding, and aesthetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical establishment
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary requirement is that arguments validly derive the conclusion from the premises; correctness of reasoning is foundational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write arguments so that each step and the overall structure are easy to follow; clarity includes correct notation, explicit hypotheses, and readable exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "Proofs tell us not only that a mathematical statement is true, but also why it is true, and they communicate this truth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to convey the reasons behind the result, not merely a formal derivation—explain mechanisms and intuitions that make the truth apparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insight and elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: "Provide whatever insight and elegance we can muster."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek proofs that illuminate structure, use clever or natural ideas, and present the argument in a concise or aesthetically pleasing way when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep understanding / transformative insight
rubrics_metrics.description: "The best proofs give us insight into the nature of mathematical reality" and create transformative moments when "a previously opaque, confounding issue becomes transparent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A top-tier proof changes the reader's conceptual grasp of the subject; aim for arguments that reveal connections and provide lasting conceptual clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem–proof format
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorem-proof format helps distinguish the claim from its proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear statement environments (theorem, lemma, corollary) separate from proofs so readers can see the precise claim before the argument; this aids comprehension and navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise theorem statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain "complete clarity about what precisely the theorem is."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State hypotheses, domain, and quantifiers exactly; avoid ambiguity about scope or assumptions so the proof addresses the correct claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose intrinsically interesting topics / organization by topic
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose topics that are intrinsically interesting to learn proof-writing on (Hamkins organises his book by topic, not method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select examples and theorems that motivate learning and illustrate key ideas; organizing material by mathematical topic rather than by abstract proof techniques helps contextualize proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs should teach (opacity → transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamkins formalises the modern teaching consensus: a proof is "good" not just when correct but when it teaches — opacity → transparency is the operative criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proofs by their pedagogical effect: does the proof transform confusion into understanding for the intended audience? Prioritize explanatory power alongside formal rigor.
